triage.name: Eczema
triage.reason: Atopic dermatitis is a very common skin condition with a characteristic distribution and history that students can diagnose clinically.

demographics: Very common in children; most cases begin before age 5
More common in people with a personal or family history of allergic disease
More common in urban and higher-income settings
Similar frequency across racial and ethnic groups, though the appearance of the rash differs with skin tone

risk_factors.text: Personal or family history of atopic disease (asthma, allergic rhinitis, food allergy)
Filaggrin gene mutations or a strong family history of eczema
Living in a dry climate or being exposed to harsh soaps and detergents
Frequent hand washing or wet work (for hand eczema)

family_history: Eczema or atopic dermatitis in a parent or sibling
Asthma or allergic rhinitis in a parent or sibling
social_history: Exposure to harsh soaps, detergents, or fragrances
Occupations involving wet work or frequent hand washing
exposures: Dust mites, pet dander, or pollen

chief_complaints.text: I have a red, dry rash
The itching is worse at night and keeps me awake
My skin feels rough and scaly

hpi.onset: Gradual, often starting in infancy or early childhood; may improve or flare over time
hpi.duration: Chronic, lasting months to years, with intermittent flares
hpi.progression: Chronic relapsing course; flares triggered by irritants, allergens, stress, or weather changes
hpi.location: Varies with age: in infants, cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces; in children and adults, flexural areas such as inside the elbows, behind the knees, neck, and hands
hpi.quality: Dry, itchy, red, scaly patches; may ooze or crust when scratched
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; itching can be intense and disrupt sleep
hpi.timing: Itching is often worse at night and in dry conditions
pertinent_negatives: Exposure to ticks or hiking in wooded areas

argues_against: Vesicles in a dermatomal distribution (herpes zoster)
Annular scaly border with central clearing (tinea)

positives.text: History of asthma or hay fever

atypical.how_it_differs: Rash often starts on the cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces; may be weepy and crusted. Itching is present but the infant may only show fussiness and poor sleep.
May present with generalized dry, itchy skin without the classic flexural rash; can be mistaken for xerosis or scabies.
Eczema may flare during pregnancy, often on the breasts, abdomen, and extremities. Must be distinguished from pregnancy-specific dermatoses like PUPPP or pemphigoid gestationis.

general.mild: Comfortable, well-appearing, no distress; skin dry but no excoriations
general.moderate: Scratching during the visit, visible excoriations, mild sleep-deprived appearance
general.severe: Restless and scratching constantly, widespread inflamed skin, appears uncomfortable
general.critical: Ill-appearing, febrile, widespread weeping or crusted skin suggesting secondary infection or erythroderma

findings.maneuver: Inspect and lightly palpate the skin over the trunk and extremities
Inspect the antecubital and popliteal fossae, neck, and wrists
findings.finding: Ill-defined erythematous, scaly patches in flexural areas

findings.maneuver: Inspect the rash for scratch marks
Palpate chronically affected areas such as the antecubital fossae
findings.finding: Thickened skin with accentuated skin markings

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces in an infant
findings.finding: Erythematous, weepy, crusted patches on the cheeks, scalp, or extensor surfaces
Extra crease below the lower eyelid

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face for periorbital darkening

findings.finding: Pale, boggy nasal turbinates suggesting allergic rhinitis

findings.maneuver: Inspect the rash for honey-colored crusts
Inspect the rash for an annular scaly border with central clearing
findings.finding: No annular border with central clearing

findings.maneuver: Inspect the rash for grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution
Inspect the oral and genital mucosa
Inspect the skin for petechiae or purpura
Inspect the rash for targetoid lesions
Palpate the cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes
findings.finding: No enlarged or tender lymph nodes

labs.caveat: Mild peripheral eosinophilia can accompany atopic dermatitis but is nonspecific and not needed for diagnosis.
Usually normal; a marked elevation should prompt consideration of another diagnosis such as a systemic inflammatory disorder or skin infection.
Usually normal; elevation suggests secondary bacterial infection or an alternative diagnosis.

initial.why: Not routinely needed; may show mild eosinophilia and helps exclude other causes of a widespread rash
initial.only_if: the diagnosis is uncertain or the rash is severe or widespread

supporting.why: Rules out tinea when the rash has a scaly annular border or does not respond to treatment
supporting.only_if: the rash is annular or fails to improve with standard eczema care

supporting.why: Shows spongiotic dermatitis; reserved for atypical, severe, or treatment-refractory cases to exclude other dermatoses
supporting.only_if: the diagnosis is unclear or the rash is refractory to therapy

supporting.why: Identifies contact allergens in suspected allergic contact dermatitis
supporting.only_if: contact dermatitis is suspected (rash limited to exposed skin or worsening with a new product)

supporting.why: Identifies the organism when secondary bacterial infection is suspected
supporting.only_if: there is weeping, honey-colored crusting, or increasing pain and redness

not_indicated.why: Not needed for a typical clinical diagnosis of eczema
Not needed for a typical clinical diagnosis of eczema
Nonspecific and does not change management
Not routinely recommended; food or aeroallergen testing does not establish the diagnosis of eczema
Should not be ordered routinely; only relevant when a true food allergy is suspected
Not part of the routine workup of typical eczema

decision_points: Eczema is a clinical diagnosis; no laboratory or imaging test confirms it
Consider KOH scraping when tinea is a possibility, since topical steroids can worsen it
Consider patch testing when contact dermatitis is suspected
Consider bacterial culture and antibiotics when secondary infection (impetiginization) is suspected

differential.name: Allergic contact dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Itchy, red, scaly rash that looks like eczema and can flare with new products

history: Rash appears only on skin that touched the trigger (e.g., nickel, fragrance, poison ivy)
Clear temporal link to a new soap, lotion, jewelry, or topical product
No personal or family history of atopy needed
exam: Sharply demarcated borders matching the area of contact
May have vesicles or bullae in acute cases
No flexural predilection unless the trigger is applied there

differential.name: Tinea corporis
differential.why_considered: Scaly, itchy, red patches that can resemble nummular eczema

history: Often starts as a single lesion and spreads outward
May have contact with pets or other people with a similar rash
Does not improve with topical steroids and may worsen
exam: Annular plaque with an active scaly border and central clearing
labs: KOH microscopy of skin scrapings shows fungal hyphae

differential.name: Psoriasis
differential.why_considered: Chronic, well-demarcated, scaly plaques that can involve flexures and be itchy

history: Plaques often on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, nails, and gluteal cleft
May have joint pain or swelling
exam: Well-demarcated salmon-colored plaques with silvery scale
Nail pitting, onycholysis, or oil spots
Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed)

differential.name: Scabies
differential.why_considered: Intensely itchy rash, worse at night, with excoriations and a similar appearance to eczema
differential.trigger: Itching that is severe at night and affects multiple family members or close contacts

history: Similar itching in household members or sexual partners
Rapid onset over days to weeks
exam: Burrows (thin, wavy lines) in web spaces, wrists, axillae, waist, or genitals
Papules or vesicles in these areas
Sparing of the face and scalp in adults (except in infants)
labs: Skin scraping with mineral oil shows mites, eggs, or feces

differential.name: Seborrheic dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Scaly, red patches on the scalp, face, and flexures that can look like eczema

history: Greasy, yellowish scale rather than dry scale
Often involves the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and presternal area
exam: Yellow, greasy scales on an erythematous base
No involvement of the antecubital or popliteal fossae

differential.name: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides)
differential.why_considered: Chronic, persistent, scaly patches or plaques that can mimic eczema and may be resistant to treatment
differential.trigger: Eczema-like rash that persists or worsens despite appropriate topical therapy, especially in an adult

history: Lesions may be on non-sun-exposed areas (buttocks, breasts, inner thighs)
No personal or family history of atopy
exam: May have poikiloderma (mottled pigmentation, telangiectasia, atrophy)
Lymphadenopathy may be present in advanced disease
labs: Skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry and T-cell receptor gene rearrangement shows atypical lymphocytes
imaging: CT or PET-CT to assess lymph nodes or visceral involvement if advanced

severity.mild: Limited areas of dry, itchy skin; minimal erythema; sleep and daily activities are not significantly affected.
severity.moderate: More extensive areas of erythema, scaling, and excoriations; itching is frequent and may disrupt sleep; some impact on daily activities.
severity.severe: Widespread involvement, intense itching, lichenification, oozing, and sleep disturbance; may have secondary infection; significant impact on quality of life.
severity.critical: Erythroderma (generalized redness and scaling over most of the body) or secondary bacterial infection with systemic signs such as fever and hypotension.

red_flags.finding: Fever with worsening rash, pain, or weeping
red_flags.meaning: Suggests secondary bacterial infection (impetiginization or cellulitis) that may require antibiotics.

red_flags.finding: Widespread redness and scaling covering most of the body
red_flags.meaning: Erythroderma, a medical emergency requiring hospitalization and systemic treatment.

red_flags.finding: Rapidly spreading redness, swelling, or tenderness
Vesicles or pustules with fever and malaise
red_flags.meaning: Possible eczema herpeticum (HSV infection), an ophthalmologic and dermatologic emergency.
Possible ocular involvement (keratoconjunctivitis) that needs urgent evaluation.

complications.name: Sleep disturbance and impaired quality of life

special_populations.differences: Rash often starts on the cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces; may be weepy and crusted. Itching may present as fussiness and poor sleep. Avoid potent topical steroids on the face and use gentle emollients.
Flexural involvement becomes more prominent after infancy. May have associated asthma or allergic rhinitis. School and sleep can be affected.
May present with generalized dry, itchy skin without classic flexural rash; can be mistaken for xerosis or scabies. Lower threshold to biopsy if atypical or treatment-resistant.

Eczema may flare during pregnancy, often on the breasts, abdomen, and extremities. Must be distinguished from pregnancy-specific dermatoses like PUPPP or pemphigoid gestationis. Topical corticosteroids are generally safe; avoid systemic steroids if possible.

key_questions.question: When did the rash start, and how has it changed over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset, often in infancy or early childhood, with a chronic relapsing course

key_questions.question: Where on your body is the rash?
key_questions.looking_for: Cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces in infants; flexural areas such as inside the elbows, behind the knees, neck, and hands in children and adults

key_questions.question: How itchy is it, and when is the itching worst?
key_questions.looking_for: Intense itching that is often worse at night and disrupts sleep

key_questions.question: What makes the rash worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Harsh soaps and detergents, wool or rough fabrics, dry air, heat and sweating, stress, scratching

key_questions.question: What makes it better?
key_questions.looking_for: Moisturizers, avoiding triggers, cool compresses, topical steroids

key_questions.question: Does the rash ooze, crust, or weep?
key_questions.looking_for: Small fluid-filled bumps that ooze or crust when scratched; new weeping or honey-colored crusts suggest secondary infection

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, or feeling generally unwell with this rash?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever with worsening rash, pain, or weeping suggests secondary bacterial infection or eczema herpeticum

key_questions.question: Do you have asthma, hay fever, or food allergies?
key_questions.looking_for: Personal history of atopic disease supports the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have eczema, asthma, or hay fever?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of atopy supports the diagnosis

key_questions.question: What soaps, lotions, detergents, or new products have you used on your skin?
key_questions.looking_for: Exposure to irritants or potential contact allergens; a clear temporal link to a new product suggests contact dermatitis

key_questions.question: Does anyone else in your household or close contacts have an itchy rash?
key_questions.looking_for: Similar itching in household members or sexual partners suggests scabies

key_questions.question: Have you started any new medications recently?
key_questions.looking_for: A new medication before rash onset suggests a drug eruption rather than eczema

key_questions.question: Have you had any blisters, mouth sores, or genital sores?
key_questions.looking_for: Mucosal involvement or blistering argues against eczema

key_questions.question: Have you had any joint pain or swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Joint symptoms suggest psoriasis or a systemic inflammatory disorder

key_questions.question: Any recent travel, tick exposure, or hiking in wooded areas?
key_questions.looking_for: Exposures that would suggest an alternative diagnosis

reasoning_points: Chronic relapsing itchy rash with dry skin
Age-appropriate distribution: cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces in infants; flexural areas in children and adults
Intense itching, often worse at night and disrupting sleep
Personal or family history of atopic disease such as asthma, allergic rhinitis, or food allergy
Examination shows xerosis with ill-defined erythematous, scaly patches, excoriations, and possibly lichenification
No fever, mucosal involvement, honey-colored crusts, annular border with central clearing, or dermatomal vesicles
Diagnosis is clinical; no laboratory or imaging test confirms it

easy: Infant or young child with itchy dry rash on the cheeks and extensor surfaces
Classic flexural rash inside the elbows and behind the knees
Personal or family history of asthma or hay fever
Symptoms improve with moisturizers and topical steroids
medium: Adult with hand eczema and no clear childhood history
Older adult with generalized dry, itchy skin without flexural involvement
Rash with excoriations and lichenification from chronic scratching
hard: Rash that persists or worsens despite appropriate topical therapy, raising concern for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
Annular scaly rash that could be tinea rather than eczema
Intensely itchy rash with similar symptoms in household members, suggesting scabies
Pregnant patient with a flare that must be distinguished from pregnancy-specific dermatoses
Rash with fever and weeping suggesting secondary bacterial infection or eczema herpeticum
